A grain is what one row of a summary stands for — one row per store, say.
Reports often need several grains at once: detail rows, subtotals, and a grand
total. `marginplyr` creates those levels with one dplyr-style summary. SQL
calls this idea `GROUPING SETS`; you do not need to know that syntax to begin.
The subtotal and total rows are the report's *margins*: in each, a column that
level removed shows the Margin label, `"Total"` by default.

This guide starts with a familiar reporting problem, then introduces
`rollup()`, `grouping_sets()`, and `cube()`. If you already know the task and
want the call, [Recipes for common reporting
tasks](https://sayuks.github.io/marginplyr/vignettes/recipes.html) is the
shorter route. Database users can continue with the [Database and lazy
backends
guide](https://sayuks.github.io/marginplyr/vignettes/database_backends.html).

## Installation

Install marginplyr from GitHub:

```{r}
#| eval: false

install.packages("pak")
pak::pkg_install("sayuks/marginplyr")
```

```{r setup}
#| message: false

library(marginplyr)
library(dplyr)
```

Nothing beyond marginplyr's own dependencies is required. Two sections below
also use an optional package — dtplyr in *Nest locally or with dtplyr* and
quartabs in *Optional Quarto tabsets with quartabs* — so their chunks evaluate
only when that package is installed at the version marginplyr asks for. Where
it is missing or too old the code is still shown, but its output is absent.

```{r}
#| include: false

# Base R translates its own diagnostics, and a rejected call shows them, so
# the page carries English whatever locale it is rendered in.
Sys.setenv(LANGUAGE = "en")

# `marginplyr_suggest_available()` answers whether an optional package is
# installed at the version marginplyr asks for.
source(system.file("suggests", "guard.R", package = "marginplyr"))

has_dtplyr <- marginplyr_suggest_available("dtplyr")
has_tabsets <- marginplyr_suggest_available("quartabs")
```

## Start with the report question

`retail_sales` contains January and February sales for 2025 and 2026 from a
fictional retail chain, so each year's total covers those two months. Each row
records one product, channel, and store combination.

```{r}
retail_sales
```

Online-direct sales do not belong to a physical store, so some source rows
have `store = NA`. This intentional missing value becomes important later:
it is a real source value, not a subtotal.

### The manual version

For January 2026, the operations team wants store detail, region subtotals,
and a company total. With ordinary summaries, each level is a separate branch
that must be aligned and combined:

```{r}
january_sales <- retail_sales |>
  filter(year == 2026L, month == "Jan")

manual_report <- bind_rows(
  january_sales |>
    summarize(revenue = sum(revenue), .by = c(region, store)),
  january_sales |>
    summarize(revenue = sum(revenue), .by = region) |>
    mutate(store = "Total") |>
    select(region, store, revenue),
  january_sales |>
    summarize(revenue = sum(revenue)) |>
    mutate(region = "Total", store = "Total") |>
    select(region, store, revenue)
)

manual_report
```

This is valid dplyr code and can be the clearest choice for one small,
one-off report. It becomes repetitive when the hierarchy grows, the requested
levels change, or every branch must stay lazy on a remote source. [Choose
the tool for the
job](https://sayuks.github.io/marginplyr/#choose-the-tool-for-the-job) on the
package home page compares it, data.table grouping sets, and the rollup
package with marginplyr.

### One Grouping plan

`rollup(region, store)` describes the same three levels directly:

```{r}
january_report <- january_sales |>
  summarize_with_margins(
    revenue = sum(revenue),
    .grouping = rollup(region, store)
  )

january_report
```

The result is one ordinary data frame. Every summary is evaluated on the source
rows of each group in each grouping set, so a subtotal's mean, distinct count
or median is computed from its own rows, never combined from the detail-level
results.

What is written in `.grouping` is a Grouping specification; the ordered list of
grouping sets it expands to is its Grouping plan.
[`inspect_grouping()`](https://sayuks.github.io/marginplyr/man/inspect_grouping.html)
returns that plan without summarizing anything, which makes it the quickest way
to check a specification:

```{r}
inspect_grouping(
  january_sales,
  .grouping = rollup(region, store)
) |>
  select(set_id, included)
```

Set 1 is the store detail, set 2 the region subtotals, and set 3 the company
total. `region` and `store` are the plan's Margin dimensions: the columns
supplied through `.grouping`, which a grouping set can remove to form a margin.
The empty set `()` means that neither dimension remains, so it produces the
grand total.

`.grouping` takes one of these constructor calls: `rollup()`,
`grouping_sets()`, `cube()`, `grouping_set()`, or `grouping_spec()`. Always
name it: written without `.grouping =`, the specification lands among the
summaries and is refused. A bare column such as `.grouping = region`, or
`.grouping = c(region, store)`, is refused too, with a message suggesting the
constructor call to write instead.

### Put subtotals next to their rows

Row order in `january_report` is unspecified. `.sort` asks for an order that
follows the Grouping plan:

```{r}
january_sales |>
  summarize_with_margins(
    revenue = sum(revenue),
    .grouping = rollup(region, store),
    .sort = "last"
  )
```

`.sort = "last"` places each subtotal after the rows it summarizes, and
`"first"` places it before them. `"none"`, the default, leaves row order
unspecified, for local and lazy inputs alike. The order comes from which
dimensions each row keeps, not from the displayed values, so neither the
`"Total"` label nor the source `NA` store decides where a row goes.
[Put each subtotal with the rows it
summarizes](https://sayuks.github.io/marginplyr/vignettes/recipes.html#put-each-subtotal-with-the-rows-it-summarizes)
shows what `.sort` does not promise; use `arrange()` for any other
presentation order.

### One independent report per month

The same hierarchy can be repeated for every reporting period without
building more branches:

```{r}
monthly_report <- retail_sales |>
  summarize_with_margins(
    units = sum(units),
    revenue = sum(revenue),
    .by = c(year, month),
    .grouping = rollup(region, store)
  )

monthly_report |>
  filter(year == 2026L, month == "Jan")
```

Columns in `.by` belong to every grouping set, so they are fixed keys rather
than Margin dimensions. They retain their input types and never receive the
Margin label. The empty set from `rollup()` still includes the fixed `.by`
columns, so it produces one company total per year and month.

### The three grouping helpers

| Helper | Mental model | Typical question |
|---|---|---|
| `rollup()` | Ordered hierarchy | “Give me stores, regions, and the company.” |
| `grouping_sets()` | Exact union of requested levels | “Give me only these views.” |
| `cube()` | Every subset | “Give me every combination of these dimensions.” |

Most reporting tasks should start with `rollup()`. Reach for
`grouping_sets()` when a hierarchy includes too much or unrelated views must
share one result. Use `cube()` deliberately: the number of grouping sets
doubles with every independent dimension.

### Extend the hierarchy through time

The review also needs monthly, per-year, and all-period totals. Moving
the period columns from `.by` into `rollup()` creates one longer hierarchy:

```{r}
all_levels <- retail_sales |>
  summarize_with_margins(
    revenue = sum(revenue),
    .grouping = rollup(year, month, region, store)
  )

all_levels |>
  filter(month == "Total")
```

The rollup expands to:

```text
(year, month, region, store)  store detail
(year, month, region)         monthly region subtotal
(year, month)                 monthly company total
(year)                        company total per year
()                            all-period company total
```

Argument order defines the hierarchy. This rollup does not create a per-year
total for each region; arbitrary grouping sets can request that separately.

## Choose the grouping operation

### Arbitrary grouping sets

Finance needs monthly company totals, region-product totals, and the overall
grand total—but no other combinations. `grouping_sets()` forms the union of
exactly those requests:

```{r}
retail_sales |>
  summarize_with_margins(
    revenue = sum(revenue),
    .grouping = grouping_sets(
      grouping_set(year, month),
      grouping_set(region, product),
      grouping_set()
    )
  )
```

An empty `grouping_set()` writes the empty set `()`.

### CUBE

Merchandising wants every subtotal across product and sales channel.
`cube(product, channel)` expands to all four subsets:

```text
(product, channel)
(product)
(channel)
()
```

```{r}
retail_sales |>
  filter(year == 2026L, month == "Jan") |>
  summarize_with_margins(
    revenue = sum(revenue),
    .grouping = cube(product, channel)
  )
```

### Union versus Cartesian product

Two rollups inside `grouping_sets()` remain independent:

```{r}
independent_totals <- retail_sales |>
  summarize_with_margins(
    revenue = sum(revenue),
    .grouping = grouping_sets(
      rollup(year, month),
      rollup(region, store)
    ),
    .duplicates = "drop"
  )

independent_totals
```

This is a union of:

```text
(year, month), (year), (), (region, store), (region)
```

Both rollups contain `()`, which is why the call above asks for `"drop"`.
Without it, the default `.duplicates = "error"` catches the overlap:

```{r}
#| label: duplicate-grouping-sets
#| error: true
#| purl: false

retail_sales |>
  summarize_with_margins(
    revenue = sum(revenue),
    .grouping = grouping_sets(
      rollup(year, month),
      rollup(region, store)
    )
  )
```

This refusal, like every error marginplyr raises for a call you can correct,
inherits the `"marginplyr_error"` class, so one `marginplyr_error` handler
catches them; *Errors and warnings* in the [package
reference](https://sayuks.github.io/marginplyr/man/marginplyr-package.html)
states the contract and the errors that need `rlang::try_fetch()`.

`"drop"` retains one copy; `"keep"` retains both copies when repeated totals
are intentionally meaningful. `.id` names an extra column numbering each row's
grouping set by its position in the Grouping plan, here `1` to `6`:

```{r}
retail_sales |>
  summarize_with_margins(
    revenue = sum(revenue),
    .grouping = grouping_sets(
      rollup(year, month),
      rollup(region, store)
    ),
    .duplicates = "keep",
    .id = "occurrence",
    .sort = "last"
  )
```

The last two rows are the `()` set of each rollup. The same dimensions are
absent from both, so only `occurrence` tells them apart. `.sort` keeps them
next to each other: `.id` breaks the remaining ties in that order, so a kept
duplicate sits beside the occurrence it repeats.

`grouping_spec()` combines the same two rollups by Cartesian product instead,
as SQL combines comma-separated grouping items: every time level crossed with
every geography level. Each rollup has three sets, so the plan has nine:

```{r}
inspect_grouping(
  retail_sales,
  .grouping = grouping_spec(
    rollup(year, month),
    rollup(region, store)
  )
) |>
  select(set_id, included)
```

### Composite dimensions and tidy-select

A `grouping_set()` nested directly inside `rollup()` or `cube()` is one
indivisible dimension. In this cube, `region` and `store` are always included
or removed together:

```{r}
inspect_grouping(
  retail_sales,
  .grouping = cube(
    grouping_set(region, store),
    all_of(c("product", "channel"))
  )
) |>
  select(set_id, included)
```

Grouping specifications accept tidy-select expressions such as `all_of()`.
They select existing columns; they do not evaluate R expressions, so
`rollup(toupper(region))` fails with `object 'region' not found`.

### Computed grouping columns

Create a computed dimension, such as `toupper(region)` or a period label, with
`mutate()` before summarizing:

```{r}
retail_sales |>
  mutate(period = paste(year, month, sep = "-")) |>
  summarize_with_margins(
    revenue = sum(revenue),
    .grouping = rollup(period, region)
  )
```

This two-step form works consistently for local and lazy tables.

## Identify totals without guessing from labels

`grouping_bit(x)` corresponds to SQL `GROUPING(x)`: it returns `1` when `x`
was removed from the current grouping set and `0` when it remains part of the
group. It does not test whether the visible value is missing.

The `_bit` suffix describes this `0`/`1` result and avoids masking the
unrelated `base::grouping()` function, which returns a permutation for placing
equal values next to one another.

```{r}
retail_sales |>
  filter(
    year == 2026L,
    month == "Jan",
    region == "East"
  ) |>
  summarize_with_margins(
    revenue = sum(revenue),
    store_is_total = grouping_bit(store),
    level = grouping_id(region, store),
    .grouping = rollup(region, store)
  )
```

The source `NA` store has `store_is_total = 0`. The region subtotal has
`store_is_total = 1`, because `store` was removed by the rollup.

The [`grouping_bit()`
reference](https://sayuks.github.io/marginplyr/man/grouping_bit.html) compares
`.id`, `inspect_grouping()$set_id`, `grouping_bit()`, and `grouping_id()` in
full. The [Grouping identity
guide](https://sayuks.github.io/marginplyr/vignettes/grouping_identity.html)
works through the same values with executable examples, and
[Recipes](https://sayuks.github.io/marginplyr/vignettes/recipes.html) uses
them to keep one grouping set and to name the set behind every row.

`grouping_id()` combines the flags as a bit mask. Its last argument is the
least-significant bit:

```text
region  store  bits  grouping_id
kept    kept    00       0
kept    total   01       1
total   total   11       3
```

Columns fixed in `.by` can also be passed to these helpers. Their flag is
always zero because they occur in every grouping set.

### Labels and column types

Change the label used for dimensions removed by aggregation:

```{r}
retail_sales |>
  summarize_with_margins(
    revenue = sum(revenue),
    .grouping = rollup(year),
    .margin_label = "All years"
  )
```

A character label changes the type of a Margin dimension that is not a
factor, so that the column can hold the label: `year` is an integer in
`retail_sales` and character in this result, and a Date dimension becomes
character the same way. A factor dimension stays a factor and gains the label
as a new level, placed last by default; `.margin_label_position = "first"`
puts it first. That changes only the level order, not the row order.

Use a named vector to give each Margin dimension its own label. Names must
cover every column `.grouping` selects exactly once; `.by` columns are fixed
keys and cannot be named:

```{r}
retail_sales |>
  summarize_with_margins(
    revenue = sum(revenue),
    .grouping = rollup(region, store),
    .margin_label = c(
      region = "All regions",
      store = "All stores"
    )
  )
```

On local data, the default `.check_margin_label = TRUE` refuses a label that
already occurs as a source value, such as a store named `"Total"`; the
[Database and lazy backends
guide](https://sayuks.github.io/marginplyr/vignettes/database_backends.html)
explains how lazy inputs and Arrow differ. A label is only a display value;
retain `grouping_bit()` or `grouping_id()` whenever source values can equal
the label.

Use `.margin_label = NULL` or `NA_character_` to preserve each Margin
dimension's input type and mark its margin rows with a typed missing Margin
value — a missing value of the column's own type — instead of a label:

```{r}
retail_sales |>
  summarize_with_margins(
    revenue = sum(revenue),
    year_is_total = grouping_bit(year),
    .grouping = rollup(year),
    .margin_label = NULL
  ) |>
  # A tibble prints each column's type: `year` is still <int>.
  as_tibble()
```

`.margin_label = NULL` and `NA_character_` are the same request: typed missing
output, with no label for `.check_margin_label` to look for among the source
values. They differ only on a factor that already has an `NA` level.
*Display labels and grouping identity* in the [`margin_verbs`
reference](https://sayuks.github.io/marginplyr/man/margin_verbs.html) gives
those cases along with the naming rules, ordered-factor preservation, and
level positioning; [Three kinds of apparent
missingness](https://sayuks.github.io/marginplyr/vignettes/grouping_identity.html#three-kinds-of-apparent-missingness)
works one factor through an NA level, a source missing value, and a
typed-missing Margin value, which can all print as `<NA>`.

## Compare a summary with its rollup parent

`share_of_parent()` divides one preceding named numeric scalar summary by its
corresponding value in the immediately less detailed rollup level:

```{r}
parent_report <- retail_sales |>
  filter(year == 2026L, month == "Jan") |>
  summarize_with_margins(
    revenue = sum(revenue),
    revenue_share = share_of_parent(revenue),
    .grouping = rollup(region, store),
    .sort = "last"
  )

parent_report
```

A row of the Grand total set has a Parent share of one. Missing numerators or
denominators and zero denominators produce a missing double value. The helper
requires a rollup and finds each row's parent from the dimensions its
grouping set removed, so displayed Margin labels and source missing keys do
not determine it.

For several measures, use two ordered `across()` expressions: the first
creates ordinary summaries and the second selects those summaries for Parent
shares.

```{r}
retail_sales |>
  filter(year == 2026L, month == "Jan") |>
  summarize_with_margins(
    across(c(units, revenue), sum),
    across(
      c(units, revenue),
      share_of_parent,
      .names = "{.col}_share"
    ),
    .grouping = rollup(region, store),
    .sort = "last"
  )
```

The [`share_of_parent()`
reference](https://sayuks.github.io/marginplyr/man/share_of_parent.html) gives
the complete rules for which summaries can be a source.

Scale, round, format, or otherwise derive from a Parent share after the Margin
summary:

```{r}
parent_report |>
  mutate(revenue_percent = 100 * revenue_share)
```

## Compare a summary with the whole

`share_of_total()` divides by a row of the Grand total set instead of the
parent level. It is written the same way, and both helpers can appear in one
summary:

```{r}
retail_sales |>
  filter(year == 2026L, month == "Jan") |>
  summarize_with_margins(
    revenue = sum(revenue),
    revenue_share = share_of_parent(revenue),
    revenue_of_total = share_of_total(revenue),
    .grouping = rollup(region, store),
    .sort = "last"
  )
```

A parent is ambiguous outside a rollup, but a grand total is not: a plan
either contains one or it does not. A `cube()` therefore has no Parent share,
and asking for one names the rewrite instead of choosing a parent:

```{r}
#| label: parent-share-outside-rollup
#| error: true
#| purl: false

retail_sales |>
  filter(year == 2026L, month == "Jan") |>
  summarize_with_margins(
    revenue = sum(revenue),
    revenue_share = share_of_parent(revenue),
    .grouping = cube(region, store)
  )
```

`share_of_total()` accepts any Grouping specification that produces a Grand
total set, that same `cube()` included:

```{r}
retail_sales |>
  filter(year == 2026L, month == "Jan") |>
  summarize_with_margins(
    revenue = sum(revenue),
    revenue_of_total = share_of_total(revenue),
    .grouping = cube(region, store),
    .sort = "last"
  )
```

A `grouping_sets()` specification qualifies only when some member produces
the empty set, such as an empty `grouping_set()` or a `rollup()`; one without
such a member is rejected:

```{r}
#| label: total-share-without-grand-total
#| error: true
#| purl: false

retail_sales |>
  filter(year == 2026L, month == "Jan") |>
  summarize_with_margins(
    revenue = sum(revenue),
    revenue_of_total = share_of_total(revenue),
    .grouping = grouping_sets(
      grouping_set(region, store),
      grouping_set(region)
    )
  )
```

Everything else is shared with `share_of_parent()` — eligible sources, the
`across()` form, and the value rules — and the
[`share_of_parent()` reference](https://sayuks.github.io/marginplyr/man/share_of_parent.html)
documents both helpers.

Which rows the denominator covers is decided by the fixed `.by` keys. [Show each
row as a percent of the
total](https://sayuks.github.io/marginplyr/vignettes/recipes.html#show-each-row-as-a-percent-of-the-total) works
through that choice.

## Complete absent keys before summarizing

A store with no sales in a month gets no row for that month, not a row of
zeros, at any level: grouping sets choose which grains to report and never
create a key the data does not contain. When such rows belong in the report,
complete the input before summarizing, locally or on a database, as the
[Complete absent keys before margins
guide](https://sayuks.github.io/marginplyr/vignettes/completing_keys.html)
shows.

## Use the same plan with remote data

The Grouping plan can be applied to a lazy table without first collecting its
rows. This PostgreSQL simulation shows the native SQL without requiring a
server. The call writes `na.rm = TRUE`, and a local call needs it too for the
results to match: locally a missing measure makes every subtotal and total that
includes it `NA`, while a SQL aggregate always drops missing values, and dbplyr
warns when `na.rm = TRUE` is absent:

```{r}
postgres_sales <- dbplyr::tbl_lazy(
  retail_sales,
  con = dbplyr::simulate_postgres()
)

postgres_sales |>
  summarize_with_margins(
    revenue = sum(revenue, na.rm = TRUE),
    .grouping = rollup(region, store)
  ) |>
  show_query()
```

The result remains lazy. Continue with [Database and lazy
backends](https://sayuks.github.io/marginplyr/vignettes/database_backends.html)
for a backend support matrix, `collect()`, live DuckDB execution, portable
`UNION ALL` SQL, and practical guidance for inspecting a query.

## Keep the detail rows

### Expand rows with `expand_with_margins()`

`expand_with_margins()` emits one copy of each source row for every grouping
set. It is useful when downstream work needs the rows rather than an
immediate summary:

```{r}
january_sales <- retail_sales |>
  filter(year == 2026L, month == "Jan")

expanded <- january_sales |>
  expand_with_margins(
    .grouping = rollup(region, store)
  )

expanded |>
  count(region, store, name = "records")
```

The same verb stays lazy for database tables, where it always uses the
portable `UNION ALL` SQL: one branch per grouping set.
[Portable fallback
SQL](https://sayuks.github.io/marginplyr/vignettes/database_backends.html#portable-fallback-sql)
in the database guide shows that query and explains its branches.

Expanded rows are also the way to compute something one aggregation pass
cannot express, which is a real limit on a database rather than a local one.
[Fix a nested-aggregate error on a
database](https://sayuks.github.io/marginplyr/vignettes/recipes.html#fix-a-nested-aggregate-error-on-a-database) works
through that case.

### Nest locally or with dtplyr

The two nesting verbs return a list column, which SQL and Arrow tables cannot
hold, so they accept local data frames and dtplyr steps only.
`nest_with_margins()` keeps one detail table for each visible group:

```{r}
nested_sections <- january_sales |>
  nest_with_margins(
    .grouping = rollup(region, store)
  )

nested_sections |>
  head()

# Inspect the source rows behind the first visible group.
nested_sections$data[[1]]
```

Use `.keep = TRUE` when the grouping keys are also needed inside each detail
table. The nested copies hold the original pre-margin values, so inside the
company total the rows keep their region and store names while the outer key shows the
Margin label:

```{r}
nested_with_keys <- january_sales |>
  nest_with_margins(
    .grouping = rollup(region, store),
    .keep = TRUE
  )

company_total <- nested_with_keys |>
  filter(region == "Total", store == "Total")

company_total$data[[1]] |>
  distinct(region, store)
```

A dtplyr input performs the expansion and nesting lazily: the result is still a
dtplyr query, which `show_query()` can display and `collect()` runs:

```{r}
#| eval: !expr has_dtplyr

nested_dt <- january_sales |>
  dtplyr::lazy_dt() |>
  nest_with_margins(
    .grouping = rollup(region, store)
  )

class(nested_dt)
collect(nested_dt)
```

`nest_by_with_margins()` returns a row-wise data frame, making one calculation
per nested report section straightforward:

```{r}
nested_by <- january_sales |>
  nest_by_with_margins(
    .grouping = rollup(region, store)
  )

nested_by |>
  mutate(
    records = nrow(data),
    units = sum(data$units),
    revenue = sum(data$revenue)
  )

nested_by$data[[1]]
```

A row-wise data frame is a local object, so `nest_by_with_margins()` collects
a dtplyr input before making it row-wise; inspect the query with the
`nest_with_margins()` form above instead:

```{r}
#| eval: !expr has_dtplyr

nested_by_dt <- january_sales |>
  dtplyr::lazy_dt() |>
  nest_by_with_margins(
    .grouping = rollup(region, store)
  )

nested_by_dt |>
  mutate(
    records = nrow(data),
    revenue = sum(data$revenue)
  )

nested_by_dt$data[[1]]
```

#### Relationship to tidyr and dplyr

The nesting verbs share the result shapes of `tidyr::nest()` and
`dplyr::nest_by()` but are not drop-in replacements; the first section of the
[`nest_with_margins()`
reference](https://sayuks.github.io/marginplyr/man/nest_with_margins.html) and
of the [`nest_by_with_margins()`
reference](https://sayuks.github.io/marginplyr/man/nest_by_with_margins.html)
lists each verb's differences.

Nesting rejects `.duplicates = "keep"`, with or without `.id`, where the value
is written rather than where a duplicate first appears:

```{r}
#| label: nesting-duplicates-keep
#| error: true
#| purl: false

january_sales |>
  nest_with_margins(
    .grouping = rollup(region, store),
    .duplicates = "keep"
  )
```

## Optional Quarto tabsets with quartabs

[`quartabs`](https://sayuks.github.io/quartabs/) can turn the nested report
sections into Quarto tabs. This compact example creates one tab per region
plus a company-total tab.

When this guide is opened as an installed package vignette, Quarto's
lightweight vignette format does not provide interactive tabsets. The same
content is displayed sequentially instead. View the
[package-site version of this guide](https://sayuks.github.io/marginplyr/vignettes/get_started.html#optional-quarto-tabsets-with-quartabs)
to use the interactive tabs.

The chunk option `results: asis` is required because `render_tabset()` emits
Quarto tabset markup.

```{r}
#| results: asis
#| eval: !expr has_tabsets

tabbed_report <- january_sales |>
  nest_by_with_margins(
    .grouping = rollup(region)
  ) |>
  mutate(
    # Order the company total before regional tabs in the rendered report.
    region = factor(region, levels = c("Total", "East", "West")),
    report = list(
      data |>
        summarize(
          records = n(),
          units = sum(units),
          revenue = sum(revenue)
        ) |>
        knitr::kable()
    )
  ) |>
  ungroup()

tabbed_report |>
  quartabs::render_tabset(
    tabset_vars = region,
    output_vars = report
  )
```

The `"Total"` tab is created by the Grouping plan. The factor's level order
makes it the first tab; `quartabs` only handles presentation, while marginplyr
defines which source rows belong to that total.

## Advanced dplyr behavior

### Persistent groups as fixed keys

Existing `dplyr::group_by()` columns act as fixed keys when `.by` is not
supplied, so this call computes the earlier `.by = c(year, month)` report and,
like every Margin verb except the row-wise `nest_by_with_margins()`, returns
ungrouped output:

```{r}
grouped_monthly_report <- retail_sales |>
  group_by(year, month) |>
  summarize_with_margins(
    units = sum(units),
    revenue = sum(revenue),
    .grouping = rollup(region, store)
  )

grouped_monthly_report |>
  filter(year == 2026L, month == "Jan")

group_vars(grouped_monthly_report)
```

Grouped input and `.by` name the fixed keys twice over, so supplying both is
refused rather than resolved in one direction:

```{r}
#| label: grouped-input-with-by
#| error: true
#| purl: false

retail_sales |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarize_with_margins(
    revenue = sum(revenue),
    .by = month,
    .grouping = rollup(region, store)
  )
```

A row-wise input is refused too; to keep its row-wise identifiers as fixed
keys, call `ungroup()` and name them in `.by`:

```{r}
rowwise_report <- retail_sales |>
  rowwise(year) |>
  ungroup() |>
  summarize_with_margins(
    revenue = sum(revenue),
    .by = year,
    .grouping = rollup(region, store)
  )

rowwise_report
```

A grouping that keeps empty groups with `.drop = FALSE` is refused rather than
completed for you:

```{r}
#| label: drop-false-groups
#| error: true
#| purl: false

retail_sales |>
  mutate(region = factor(region)) |>
  group_by(region, .drop = FALSE) |>
  summarize_with_margins(
    revenue = sum(revenue),
    .grouping = rollup(store)
  )
```

When those empty keys belong in the report, complete the input before the
Margin operation, as [Complete absent keys before
margins](https://sayuks.github.io/marginplyr/vignettes/completing_keys.html)
shows. *Grouped and row-wise inputs* in the [`margin_verbs`
reference](https://sayuks.github.io/marginplyr/man/margin_verbs.html) states
the rule for all four verbs.

### Intentional differences from `dplyr::summarize()`

Summary expressions use dplyr data masking, but `across()` and `pick()`
exclude every column of the Grouping plan, so `everything()` below selects
neither the fixed key `year` nor the Margin dimensions `region` and `store`:

```{r}
retail_sales |>
  summarize_with_margins(
    total = sum(revenue),
    selected = toString(names(pick(everything()))),
    .by = year,
    .grouping = rollup(region, store)
  ) |>
  distinct(selected)
```

On a local data frame, a later `across()` or `pick()` sees summaries already
computed in the same call, as `total` above and here; on a lazy input the
backend decides, and marginplyr does not collect the data to provide the local
behavior:

```{r}
data.frame(region = c("East", "West"), value = c(1, 2)) |>
  summarize_with_margins(
    total = sum(value),
    across(total, ~ .x * 2, .names = "double_{.col}"),
    .grouping = rollup(region)
  )
```

The `cur_group*()` family has no meaning once several grouping sets are
combined, so it is refused with a marginplyr error naming `grouping_bit()` and
`grouping_id()` as the replacement:

```{r}
#| label: cur-group-id-rejected
#| error: true
#| purl: false

retail_sales |>
  summarize_with_margins(
    branch = cur_group_id(),
    .grouping = cube(region, channel)
  )
```

*Relationship to dplyr summaries* in the [`summarize_with_margins()`
reference](https://sayuks.github.io/marginplyr/man/summarize_with_margins.html)
states each of these rules in full, with the ones this guide does not show.
